Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.

**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in de

New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a st
- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.

### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until t

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a st
- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.

### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until t

The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;

# Plan for #230: a web control surface on the remote port

One commit. The app runs at every step of the order at the end. "Facts"
below is `facts.md` for this ticket, cited as `facts:<line>`. Tree
references were checked in the worktree at "Release 0.4.1".

## Where this departs from the issue

1. **The excerpt is not on the wire.** The issue gives each session "the
   one-line excerpt the card shows". `SessionView`
   (`control/src/lib.rs:637`) has no excerpt field and `last_message`,
   which `docs/remote-client.md` §4.3 (`session.last_response` bullet)
   calls "a field of the session's metadata", exists nowhere in the
   wire crate (facts:8). The card's line is drawn on the Mac by
   `caption_of` (`src/app.rs:4105`). Owner question 6 (facts:91) is
   unanswered, so the plan builds its "no" branch: a row shows the
   session's name, kind, card word and waiting reason. The branch
   the other way is an additive `excerpt: Option<String>` on
   `SessionView` with `#[serde(default)]`, a `changed {session}` that
   already follows the fingerprint, and a regenerated
   `client/Fixtures/session*.json`; it is not built here.
2. **The page cannot learn its scope from anything.** The issue puts
   "the device's scope" in the header and hides the reply box without
   `control`. No endpoint says it (facts:9), though `docs/remote-client.md`
   §5 ("the host answers with the device's scope") says every reply
   does; the envelope carries only `epoch`, `revision` and `body`
   (`src/app.rs:3730`). Owner question 7 (facts:94) is unanswered; the
   plan builds its "yes": `GET /api/v1/device`. The "no" branch (the
   page stores the scope from the `/pair` reply and learns of a change
   from a 403) is worse for a page, whose cookie it cannot read, so
   it is not built.
3. **"Revoked" cannot come from the host.** A revoked token and an
   unknown one get the same 401 and `devices.json` keeps no tombstone
   (facts:10; `authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3127`; `RevokeDevice`,
   `src/core/remote.rs:86`). Owner question 5 (facts:88) is
   unanswered; the plan builds the "no" branch with a twist that
   needs no record: the page remembers, in `localStorage`, that it
   paired with this `server_id` and key. A 401 on a browser that
   remembers pairing says "this device was revoked on the Mac, or the
   Mac forgot every pairing; pair again", and a 401 on one that does
   not says "not paired". The tombstone branch (a durable
   `revoked.json` of token hashes, beside `devices.json`, written
   through `RemoteFiles::save`) is not built.
4. **The `key` check is against a field the answering server writes.**
   The issue has the page "compare the key in the URL with the one
   `/info` presents". A page cannot read the TLS certificate or its
   SPKI (facts:67, unresolved; the plan assumes it cannot), so the
   comparison is with the `spki_sha256` field of `/info`'s JSON. It
   stops a page reaching the wrong genuine Switchboard by address; it
   stops no impostor. See decision 1.
5. **There is no all-sessions read.** "Sessions grouped by project"
   costs `GET /projects` and one `GET /projects/{id}/sessions` per
   project (facts:9); the page does them one at a time (see the
   signals). No new read model.
6. **"The host's own HTTP client as the CLI does".** The CLI
   (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:106`) is Swift. The
   Rust test side is the hand-rolled `http` in `tests/remote.rs:245`,
   which reads only the status and `Content-Length` (facts:19). The
   plan extends that helper; it adds no client to `src/`.
7. **Device names.** The issue wants "Safari on iPhone" from the user
   agent. The host reads no `User-Agent` and does not need to: `/pair`
   already takes `device_name` from the body (`src/app.rs:3650`,
   facts:14), so the page builds the name. An iPad's Safari sends a
   Mac's user agent (facts:59), so the page tells it apart with
   `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1`, a heuristic the plan states in the
   code's comment; a wrong guess only mislabels a row the owner can
   see. Owner question 10 (facts:101) is open; its other branch (the
   page asks for a typed name) is a field on the pairing view and is
   not built.
8. **A correction to the investigation notes, not to the issue.** The
   notes count about 28 `RemoteReply { .. }` literals; there are ten
   (`src/app.rs:1664, 1679, 2365, 2371, 2376, 2754, 3570, 3723, 3736,
   3767`), the rest of the matches are signatures.

## The record

Nothing on disk changes. A browser is a `PairedDevice`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:96`) like any other: name from the page, scope
from the pairing window, listed and revoked in the existing dialog. No
field is added to `PairedDevice` or `Identity`, so no
`IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` change (1 today, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`)
and none to `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`) or
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `:612`); `model.rs` is not touched. If an
owner answer flips a branch above and a field is needed after all
(owner question 9's separate web switch would put `web: bool` with
`#[serde(default)]` on `Listen`), the bump is the value in
`src/ports/remote.rs` at implementation time, plus one, because a
ticket landing in parallel may take the next number first; there is no
migrate step for either file (`devices.json` and `identity.json` load
with plain serde, facts:15).

What the page keeps, per device, none of it from a host's data:
the cookie (set by the host, `HttpOnly`, so script cannot read it) and
one `localStorage` entry `sb.host = {server_id, spki_sha256}` written
after a successful pairing, which is how decision 1's check and
revoked-versus-never-paired are said. `localStorage` is wrapped in
`try`/`catch`; without it the page works and says "not paired" instead
of "revoked". Everything else is refetched on every load, as the Swift
client does (`docs/remote-client.md` §7, "What the client keeps").

## The signals

The wire gains three static paths, one route, one request field, and
one authentication source. `REMOTE_PROTOCOL` stays 1: every addition is
additive.

**Decision 1: browser trust in the self-signed certificate. Option A: the
click-through on the local network is the trust step.**
This rests on two lines. The certificate has no SAN, no `serverAuth`
EKU and a year-4096 expiry (facts:16), and iOS trusts only a certificate
that names the server in the SAN, carries the EKU and lives 825 days or
less (facts:55), so option B (the host offers its certificate) is a new
certificate per LAN address, a profile install and Certificate Trust
Settings on each device (facts:54) for a thing the owner does once per
phone anyway. And whether Safari lets a WebSocket through after the
page's click-through is unresolved (facts:64, bug 145819); only a device
settles it. That is owner question 1 (facts:76), and it decides
nothing about the build: **the page falls back to polling if the
socket fails to open** (below), which is the fallback facts:78 names
for Safari. Option B stays unbuilt; if the owner's device run wants it,
the work is `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`) issuing the
certificate with the address in its SAN and the EKU, from the same key
so every native pin holds (facts:55, the pin hashes the key), and a
download path.
What option A buys: the connection is encrypted against anyone
watching the LAN, and the `key` in the URL stops a page that reached
the wrong genuine Switchboard (a reused DHCP address, two Macs) from
sending the code. What it does not buy: a page served by an active
impostor is not a genuine page, and an impostor can relay `/pair` to
the real host inside the window and keep the cookie the real host sets.
Doing that needs a man in the middle of the Mac's address and the owner
clicking through the warning for it within five minutes. The dialog
says so (see the UI). `docs/remote-client.md` §5's "the client verifies
the pin on every connection" gains "a browser cannot; see §5.1".

**Decision 2: the token reaches the socket in a cookie. Cookie, with the
Origin rule below; the bearer header stays for the native clients.**
The owner's question 2 (facts:79) is open; the plan takes the cookie
branch because it keeps the token out of script and out of the storage
Safari prunes after seven days (facts:58), and the browser sends it on
the WebSocket handshake (facts:30), which a subprotocol would need
`respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519`) to echo (facts:34).
- `POST /api/v1/pair` takes a new body field `web: true`. The
  reply for a web pairing carries no `token` in the body (script never
  sees it) and sets
  `sb-<server_id>=<token>; Path=/api/v1; Max-Age=34560000; HttpOnly;
  Secure; SameSite=Strict`. The name carries the `server_id` because
  cookies are not isolated by port (facts:24), so two instances on one
  address (the dev aid `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, the tests) must not
  share one. `Path=/api/v1` keeps the cookie off the static requests.
  Without `web` the reply is today's, byte for byte, and no
  `Set-Cookie` is sent.
- `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) reads the bearer if present and
  ignores any cookie then; with no bearer it reads the cookie named
  for this host's `server_id`. A request whose credential came from the
  cookie must pass the **Origin rule**: for a non-`GET` request or an
  upgrade, `Origin` must equal `https://` plus the request's `Host`
  header, else 403 `origin`. The rule is needed because `SameSite`
  ignores the port, so a page on another port of this IP is same-site
  (facts:25), and the browser sends `Origin` on every POST and every
  socket handshake (facts:31, 32). A `GET` carries none (facts:32),
  and the rule does not cover it: a cross-origin page cannot read a
  `GET`'s reply (the port never sends a CORS header, and answers no
  `OPTIONS`), and no `GET` route changes a record (the route table,
  `src/app.rs:3027-3110`). The bearer path needs no rule: a
  cross-origin page cannot attach the header.
- A 401 for a cookie credential the host does not know also sends
  `sb-<server_id>=; Path=/api/v1; Max-Age=0`, so a revoked device's
  browser stops sending a dead cookie on every poll.
- The cookie's `Secure` and `HttpOnly` on a click-through origin are
  stored and sent per the standard (facts:27) but no vendor says
  Safari or Chrome do (facts:65). If a device does not keep it, the
  page's first call after pairing (`GET /device`) is a 401 and the page
  says "this browser would not keep the pairing; open the pairing window
  and try again", having spent the code. The fallback the implementer
  builds if the owner's device run shows this is a follow-up, not this
  commit: the `web` field takes `"token"`, the reply carries the token,
  the page holds it in `localStorage` (and so loses it after seven
  days idle, facts:58), sends `Authorization: Bearer` on fetch, and
  polls because the socket cannot carry it. No host change beyond the
  field's third value. This is stated so the owner can pick it with
  the device result in hand.

**New route** `GET /api/v1/device`, authenticated, any scope: body
`{ "device_id", "name", "scope" }` of the caller, in the usual envelope
(`authenticated: true`). It is added to the route table in
`serve_remote` after `authenticate`, answered by `remote_device(&self,
&PairedDevice)`. The scope is read from the core on every call, so a
change in the dialog shows on the page's next request, as §5 says.
Not added to `info.capabilities`: that list is in `client/Fixtures/info.json`
and the Swift tests decode it.

**Decision 4: static paths** — `GET /`, `GET /app.js`, `GET /app.css`
and nothing else. `/index.html`, `/favicon.ico` and every other path
outside `/api/v1/` stay `404 not_found` from `serve_remote`
(`src/app.rs:3023`), so `tests/remote.rs:464` holds. A query string on
the three is ignored (the pairing link is `/?code=...`). A method other
than `GET` is 405 with `Allow: GET`. Each answer is `200` with
- `Content-Type`: `text/html; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`, `text/css; charset=utf-8`;
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src data:; base-uri
  'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. No inline
  script, no inline style, no external resource. `default-src` does not
  cover the last three (facts:41) and `frame-ancestors` works only as
  a header (facts:42), so they are listed. `img-src data:` is for the
  page's `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">`, which saves a
  `/favicon.ico` request. `connect-src 'self'` covers `wss:` to the
  page's own host and port in the spec (facts:39); older Safari builds
  are unresolved (facts:68). If one blocks it the socket fails and the
  poll fallback runs, the same path as a Safari certificate failure;
- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. The page's own subresource
  requests are made while the URL still carries the code, and a same-origin
  `Referer` is the full URL by default (facts:48); this header on the
  HTML is what keeps `/app.js` and `/app.css` from sending it;
- `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a page never outlives its version, and
  `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`;
- `Connection: close`.

*Where they are answered.* On the connection thread, before the frame
hand-off in `connection` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:795`), as the 429 and
503 already are. The files are compile-time bytes, so no frame state is
read, the frame's 64-deep inbox and 8-per-pass drain are not spent on
them (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.1: "the frame does core state only"),
and the code in a `/?code=` request line never reaches the frame's
memory or a `log::` call. Neither `connection` nor `RemoteRequest`'s
Debug output is logged today; the adapter must keep it so, and a test
asserts the page's request never produces a `refuse` line (the page
paths do not reach it).
*Pool and rate.* A page load is an unauthenticated connection like
`/info`'s, so it sits in the 4-slot pool (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`,
`src/adapters/remote.rs:567`); `Connection: close` returns the slot
as soon as the file is written, so a load holds a slot for a few
milliseconds rather than the 30-second idle timeout, and the
HTTP/1.1-without-ALPN fan-out (facts:17, 71) cannot wedge the pool.
How many connections a given browser opens is unmeasured (facts:71);
the spike records it. A new `Limits.page` window, 60 a minute per
listener like `/info` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:623`), counts the
three paths together and answers 429 beyond it. The paired pool is 12
shared with the headset and the CLI, and a tab holds one slot for its
socket; the page therefore fetches **one request at a time** (a small
queue in `app.js`), so a tab holds at most a socket and one fetch
connection.
*With no code and no token* the page shows a static "Pair from the Mac"
panel and no host name; the same bytes go to everyone and the page
makes no request to find out who answers. This is the "a page" branch
of owner question 8 (facts:97). The "nothing" branch is `asset("/")`
returning `None`, one line. *Both binds serve it.* The files carry no
host data, so there is nothing to withhold on a loopback bind, and the
LAN rule of §5 becomes: before pairing a non-loopback bind serves
`/info`, `/pair` and these three files, which hold no host data. Owner
question 9 (facts:100) is open; the branch of a separate web switch is
a `web: bool` on `Listen` (see the record) and an arm in `connection`.

**The page's protocol** is the one the headset speaks, `docs/remote-client.md`
§4.4, re-implemented in `web/app.js`:
1. Open with `?code&key&id`: before any `await`, read the three,
   then `history.replaceState(null, "", location.pathname)`
   (allowed for the path and query of an https URL and it replaces the
   entry rather than adding one, facts:45, 46). The browser's global
   history, a camera app's prefetch and a link scanner may see the URL
   first and are unresolved (facts:69, 70); the code is single-use
   (facts:11), so what they keep is dead once the device pairs. The
   query form is the issue's; owner question 4 (facts:85) is open, and
   the fragment branch is `location.hash` in the page and a `#` for
   `?` in the one function that builds the link: the plan keeps the
   query and adds `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` as facts:87 asks.
2. `GET /api/v1/info`; refuse and send nothing if `spki_sha256` or
   `server_id` differs from the link's ("this is not the Mac whose code
   was shown"). Then `POST /api/v1/pair` with `{code, spki_sha256,
   device_name, web: true}`. `403 pairing_closed` is "the pairing window
   on the Mac is closed; open it again". Write `sb.host`.
3. Opened without a link: read `sb.host`; `GET /info`; if its
   `server_id` or key differs from `sb.host`, say "identity changed,
   pair again" and stop (the spec's wording, §5) before sending
   anything else.
4. `GET /api/v1/device`: 401 is "revoked" if `sb.host` is set, else
   "not paired"; 503 `full` is "the Mac has too many connections open".
5. Open `wss` at `/api/v1/events` by a relative URL (resolved against
   the page, facts:36). Wait for `hello`, then snapshot (`projects`, then
   each `projects/{id}/sessions`), then apply the buffered events, per
   "Subscribe first, then snapshot". One held revision per key
   (`projects`, `sessions:<project>`, `session:<id>`, `waiting`,
   `conversation:<id>`, `screen:<id>`); a reply is applied only at or
   past the held revision; a new `epoch` drops everything;
   `changed` past the held revision refetches that key; `removed` drops
   it; `resync_required` or a close reconnects with 1 s doubling to 30 s,
   and a close followed by a 401 is the revoked state, which is how a
   revocation in the dialog (it drops the subscriber's queue,
   `src/app.rs:486`) reaches the page at once.
6. The open session sends `{"type":"watch","resource":{"kind":
   "conversation"|"screen","id":<record id>}}` (the frame format at
   `src/app.rs:1704-1735`), fetches after `watching`, and sends
   `unwatch` when closed. A visible content view also refetches every
   thirty seconds, as §4.4 says.
7. **Poll fallback** (the cost of owner question 1's other answer): if
   the socket gives no `hello` within five seconds on two attempts in a
   row, or `connect-src` reports a violation, the page says "Live
   updates are off; refreshing every 3 seconds" and refetches `waiting`,
   the project lists and the open view every three seconds, applying by
   revision as before. It retries the socket on a reload only.
8. Send: `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}`, `op` a
   fresh UUID per attempt held until the reply; after a timeout the page
   reads `GET /api/v1/ops/{op}` and never resends blind (§4.5). Shown
   only when `device.scope` is `control`; a 403 `scope` hides it and
   re-reads `/device`. The 16 KiB cap is `info.limits.send_bytes`.

## Actions and effects

No `AppAction`, no `Effect` and no port trait changes. The core is not
involved except for one pure function: pairing is an adapter and frame
matter, and `AppAction::Paired` and `RevokeDevice` already do the whole
record. Everything below is adapter and frame.

- `src/adapters/remote.rs`

    read in `read_request` (`:444`) from the lowercased headers beside
    `authorization`. `read_request` is the only place that builds one.

    in `src/app.rs` and the two in the adapter get `set_cookie: None`.

# Plan for #230: a web control surface on the remote port

One commit. The app runs at every step of the order at the end. "Facts"
below is `facts.md` for this ticket, cited as `facts:<line>`. Tree
references were checked in the worktree at "Release 0.4.1".

## Where this departs from the issue

1. **The excerpt is not on the wire.** The issue gives each session "the
   one-line excerpt the card shows". `SessionView`
   (`control/src/lib.rs:637`) has no excerpt field and `last_message`,
   which `docs/remote-client.md` §4.3 (`session.last_response` bullet)
   calls "a field of the session's metadata", exists nowhere in the
   wire crate (facts:8). The card's line is drawn on the Mac by
   `caption_of` (`src/app.rs:4105`). Owner question 6 (facts:91) is
   unanswered, so the plan builds its "no" branch: a row shows the
   session's name, kind, card word and waiting reason. The branch
   the other way is an additive `excerpt: Option<String>` on
   `SessionView` with `#[serde(default)]`, a `changed {session}` that
   already follows the fingerprint, and a regenerated
   `client/Fixtures/session*.json`; it is not built here.
2. **The page cannot learn its scope from anything.** The issue puts
   "the device's scope" in the header and hides the reply box without
   `control`. No endpoint says it (facts:9), though `docs/remote-client.md`
   §5 ("the host answers with the device's scope") says every reply
   does; the envelope carries only `epoch`, `revision` and `body`
   (`src/app.rs:3730`). Owner question 7 (facts:94) is unanswered; the
   plan builds its "yes": `GET /api/v1/device`. The "no" branch (the
   page stores the scope from the `/pair` reply and learns of a change
   from a 403) is worse for a page, whose cookie it cannot read, so
   it is not built.
3. **"Revoked" cannot come from the host.** A revoked token and an
   unknown one get the same 401 and `devices.json` keeps no tombstone
   (facts:10; `authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3127`; `RevokeDevice`,
   `src/core/remote.rs:86`). Owner question 5 (facts:88) is
   unanswered; the plan builds the "no" branch with a twist that
   needs no record: the page remembers, in `localStorage`, that it
   paired with this `server_id` and key. A 401 on a browser that
   remembers pairing says "this device was revoked on the Mac, or the
   Mac forgot every pairing; pair again", and a 401 on one that does
   not says "not paired". The tombstone branch (a durable
   `revoked.json` of token hashes, beside `devices.json`, written
   through `RemoteFiles::save`) is not built.
4. **The `key` check is against a field the answering server writes.**
   The issue has the page "compare the key in the URL with the one
   `/info` presents". A page cannot read the TLS certificate or its
   SPKI (facts:67, unresolved; the plan assumes it cannot), so the
   comparison is with the `spki_sha256` field of `/info`'s JSON. It
   stops a page reaching the wrong genuine Switchboard by address; it
   stops no impostor. See decision 1.
5. **There is no all-sessions read.** "Sessions grouped by project"
   costs `GET /projects` and one `GET /projects/{id}/sessions` per
   project (facts:9); the page does them one at a time (see the
   signals). No new read model.
6. **"The host's own HTTP client as the CLI does".** The CLI
   (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:106`) is Swift. The
   Rust test side is the hand-rolled `http` in `tests/remote.rs:245`,
   which reads only the status and `Content-Length` (facts:19). The
   plan extends that helper; it adds no client to `src/`.
7. **Device names.** The issue wants "Safari on iPhone" from the user
   agent. The host reads no `User-Agent` and does not need to: `/pair`
   already takes `device_name` from the body (`src/app.rs:3650`,
   facts:14), so the page builds the name. An iPad's Safari sends a
   Mac's user agent (facts:59), so the page tells it apart with
   `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1`, a heuristic the plan states in the

## The record

Nothing on disk changes. A browser is a `PairedDevice`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:96`) like any other: name from the page, scope
from the pairing window, listed and revoked in the existing dialog. No
field is added to `PairedDevice` or `Identity`, so no
`IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` change (1 today, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`)
and none to `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`) or
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `:612`); `model.rs` is not touched. If an
owner answer flips a branch above and a field is needed after all
(owner question 9's separate web switch would put `web: bool` with
`#[serde(default)]` on `Listen`), the bump is the value in
`src/ports/remote.rs` at implementation time, plus one, because a
ticket landing in parallel may take the next number first; there is no
migrate step for either file (`devices.json` and `identity.json` load
with plain serde, facts:15).

What the page keeps, per device, none of it from a host's data:
the cookie (set by the host, `HttpOnly`, so script cannot read it) and
one `localStorage` entry `sb.host = {server_id, spki_sha256}` written
after a successful pairing, which is how decision 1's check and
revoked-versus-never-paired are said. `localStorage` is wrapped in
`try`/`catch`; without it the page works and says "not paired" instead
of "revoked". Everything else is refetched on every load, as the Swift
client does (`docs/remote-client.md` §7, "What the client keeps").

## The signals

The wire gains three static paths, one route, one request field, and
one authentication source. `REMOTE_PROTOCOL` stays 1: every addition is
additive.

**Decision 1: browser trust in the self-signed certificate. Option A: the
click-through on the local network is the trust step.**
This rests on two lines. The certificate has no SAN, no `serverAuth`
EKU and a year-4096 expiry (facts:16), and iOS trusts only a certificate
that names the server in the SAN, carries the EKU and lives 825 days or
less (facts:55), so option B (the host offers its certificate) is a new
certificate per LAN address, a profile install and Certificate Trust
Settings on each device (facts:54) for a thing the owner does once per
phone anyway. And whether Safari lets a WebSocket through after the
page's click-through is unresolved (facts:64, bug 145819); only a device
settles it. That is owner question 1 (facts:76), and it decides
nothing about the build: **the page falls back to polling if the
socket fails to open** (below), which is the fallback facts:78 names
for Safari. Option B stays unbuilt; if the owner's device run wants it,
the work is `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`) issuing the
certificate with the address in its SAN and the EKU, from the same key
so every native pin holds (facts:55, the pin hashes the key), and a
download path.
What option A buys: the connection is encrypted against anyone
watching the LAN, and the `key` in the URL stops a page that reached
the wrong genuine Switchboard (a reused DHCP address, two Macs) from
sending the code. What it does not buy: a page served by an active
impostor is not a genuine page, and an impostor can relay `/pair` to
the real host inside the window and keep the cookie the real host sets.
Doing that needs a man in the middle of the Mac's address and the owner
clicking through the warning for it within five minutes. The dialog
says so (see the UI). `docs/remote-client.md` §5's "the client verifies
the pin on every connection" gains "a browser cannot; see §5.1".

**Decision 2: the token reaches the socket in a cookie. Cookie, with the
Origin rule below; the bearer header stays for the native clients.**
The owner's question 2 (facts:79) is open; the plan takes the cookie
branch because it keeps the token out of script and out of the storage
Safari prunes after seven days (facts:58), and the browser sends it on
the WebSocket handshake (facts:30), which a subprotocol would need
`respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519`) to echo (facts:34).
- `POST /api/v1/pair` takes a new body field `web: true`. The
  reply for a web pairing carries no `token` in the body (script never
  sees it) and sets
  `sb-<server_id>=<token>; Path=/api/v1; Max-Age=34560000; HttpOnly;
  Secure; SameSite=Strict`. The name carries the `server_id` because
  cookies are not isolated by port (facts:24), so two instances on one
  address (the dev aid `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, the tests) must not
  share one. `Path=/api/v1` keeps the cookie off the static requests.
  Without `web` the reply is today's, byte for byte, and no
  `Set-Cookie` is sent.
- `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) reads the bearer if present and
  ignores any cookie then; with no bearer it reads the cookie named
  for this host's `server_id`. A request whose credential came from the
  cookie must pass the **Origin rule**: for a non-`GET` request or an
  upgrade, `Origin` must equal `https://` plus the request's `Host`
  header, else 403 `origin`. The rule is needed because `SameSite`
  ignores the port, so a page on another port of this IP is same-site
  (facts:25), and the browser sends `Origin` on every POST and every
  socket handshake (facts:31, 32). A `GET` carries none (facts:32),
  and the rule does not cover it: a cross-origin page cannot read a
  `GET`'s reply (the port never sends a CORS header, and answers no
  `OPTIONS`), and no `GET` route changes a record (the route table,
  `src/app.rs:3027-3110`). The bearer path needs no rule: a
  cross-origin page cannot attach the header.
- A 401 for a cookie credential the host does not know also sends
  `sb-<server_id>=; Path=/api/v1; Max-Age=0`, so a revoked device's
  browser stops sending a dead cookie on every poll.
- The cookie's `Secure` and `HttpOnly` on a click-through origin are
  stored and sent per the standard (facts:27) but no vendor says
  Safari or Chrome do (facts:65). If a device does not keep it, the
  page's first call after pairing (`GET /device`) is a 401 and the page
  says "this browser would not keep the pairing; open the pairing window
  and try again", having spent the code. The fallback the implementer
  builds if the owner's device run shows this is a follow-up, not this
  commit: the `web` field takes `"token"`, the reply carries the token,
  the page holds it in `localStorage` (and so loses it after seven
  days idle, facts:58), sends `Authorization: Bearer` on fetch, and
  polls because the socket cannot carry it. No host change beyond the
  field's third value. This is stated so the owner can pick it with
  the device result in hand.

**New route** `GET /api/v1/device`, authenticated, any scope: body
`{ "device_id", "name", "scope" }` of the caller, in the usual envelope
(`authenticated: true`). It is added to the route table in
`serve_remote` after `authenticate`, answered by `remote_device(&self,
&PairedDevice)`. The scope is read from the core on every call, so a
change in the dialog shows on the page's next request, as §5 says.
Not added to `info.capabilities`: that list is in `client/Fixtures/info.json`
and the Swift tests decode it.

**Decision 4: static paths** — `GET /`, `GET /app.js`, `GET /app.css`
and nothing else. `/index.html`, `/favicon.ico` and every other path
outside `/api/v1/` stay `404 not_found` from `serve_remote`
(`src/app.rs:3023`), so `tests/remote.rs:464` holds. A query string on
the three is ignored (the pairing link is `/?code=...`). A method other
than `GET` is 405 with `Allow: GET`. Each answer is `200` with
- `Content-Type`: `text/html; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`, `text/css; charset=utf-8`;
- `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self';
  style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src data:; base-uri
  'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. No inline
  script, no inline style, no external resource. `default-src` does not
  cover the last three (facts:41) and `frame-ancestors` works only as
  a header (facts:42), so they are listed. `img-src data:` is for the
  page's `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">`, which saves a
  `/favicon.ico` request. `connect-src 'self'` covers `wss:` to the
  page's own host and port in the spec (facts:39); older Safari builds
  are unresolved (facts:68). If one blocks it the socket fails and the
  poll fallback runs, the same path as a Safari certificate failure;
- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. The page's own subresource
  requests are made while the URL still carries the code, and a same-origin
  `Referer` is the full URL by default (facts:48); this header on the
  HTML is what keeps `/app.js` and `/app.css` from sending it;
- `Cache-Control: no-store`, so a page never outlives its version, and
  `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`;
- `Connection: close`.

*Where they are answered.* On the connection thread, before the frame
hand-off in `connection` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:795`), as the 429 and
503 already are. The files are compile-time bytes, so no frame state is
read, the frame's 64-deep inbox and 8-per-pass drain are not spent on
them (`docs/remote-client.md` §4.1: "the frame does core state only"),
and the code in a `/?code=` request line never reaches the frame's
memory or a `log::` call. Neither `connection` nor `RemoteRequest`'s
Debug output is logged today; the adapter must keep it so, and a test
asserts the page's request never produces a `refuse` line (the page
paths do not reach it).
*Pool and rate.* A page load is an unauthenticated connection like
`/info`'s, so it sits in the 4-slot pool (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`,
`src/adapters/remote.rs:567`); `Connection: close` returns the slot
as soon as the file is written, so a load holds a slot for a few
milliseconds rather than the 30-second idle timeout, and the
HTTP/1.1-without-ALPN fan-out (facts:17, 71) cannot wedge the pool.
How many connections a given browser opens is unmeasured (facts:71);
the spike records it. A new `Limits.page` window, 60 a minute per
listener like `/info` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:623`), counts the
three paths together and answers 429 beyond it. The paired pool is 12
shared with the headset and the CLI, and a tab holds one slot for its
socket; the page therefore fetches **one request at a time** (a small
queue in `app.js`), so a tab holds at most a socket and one fetch
connection.
*With no code and no token* the page shows a static "Pair from the Mac"
panel and no host name; the same bytes go to everyone and the page
makes no request to find out who answers. This is the "a page" branch
of owner question 8 (facts:97). The "nothing" branch is `asset("/")`
returning `None`, one line. *Both binds serve it.* The files carry no
host data, so there is nothing to withhold on a loopback bind, and the
LAN rule of §5 becomes: before pairing a non-loopback bind serves
`/info`, `/pair` and these three files, which hold no host data. Owner
question 9 (facts:100) is open; the branch of a separate web switch is
a `web: bool` on `Listen` (see the record) and an arm in `connection`.

**The page's protocol** is the one the headset speaks, `docs/remote-client.md`
§4.4, re-implemented in `web/app.js`:
1. Open with `?code&key&id`: before any `await`, read the three,
   then `history.replaceState(null, "", location.pathname)`
   (allowed for the path and query of an https URL and it replaces the
   entry rather than adding one, facts:45, 46). The browser's global
   history, a camera app's prefetch and a link scanner may see the URL
   first and are unresolved (facts:69, 70); the code is single-use
   (facts:11), so what they keep is dead once the device pairs. The
   query form is the issue's; owner question 4 (facts:85) is open, and
   the fragment branch is `location.hash` in the page and a `#` for
   `?` in the one function that builds the link: the plan keeps the
   query and adds `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` as facts:87 asks.
2. `GET /api/v1/info`; refuse and send nothing if `spki_sha256` or
   `server_id` differs from the link's ("this is not the Mac whose code
   was shown"). Then `POST /api/v1/pair` with `{code, spki_sha256,
   device_name, web: true}`. `403 pairing_closed` is "the pairing window
   on the Mac is closed; open it again". Write `sb.host`.
3. Opened without a link: read `sb.host`; `GET /info`; if its
   `server_id` or key differs from `sb.host`, say "identity changed,
   pair again" and stop (the spec's wording, §5) before sending
   anything else.
4. `GET /api/v1/device`: 401 is "revoked" if `sb.host` is set, else
   "not paired"; 503 `full` is "the Mac has too many connections open".
5. Open `wss` at `/api/v1/events` by a relative URL (resolved against
   the page, facts:36). Wait for `hello`, then snapshot (`projects`, then
   each `projects/{id}/sessions`), then apply the buffered events, per
   "Subscribe first, then snapshot". One held revision per key
   (`projects`, `sessions:<project>`, `session:<id>`, `waiting`,
   `conversation:<id>`, `screen:<id>`); a reply is applied only at or
   past the held revision; a new `epoch` drops everything;
   `changed` past the held revision refetches that key; `removed` drops
   it; `resync_required` or a close reconnects with 1 s doubling to 30 s,
   and a close followed by a 401 is the revoked state, which is how a
   revocation in the dialog (it drops the subscriber's queue,
   `src/app.rs:486`) reaches the page at once.
6. The open session sends `{"type":"watch","resource":{"kind":
   "conversation"|"screen","id":<record id>}}` (the frame format at
   `src/app.rs:1704-1735`), fetches after `watching`, and sends
   `unwatch` when closed. A visible content view also refetches every
   thirty seconds, as §4.4 says.
7. **Poll fallback** (the cost of owner question 1's other answer): if
   the socket gives no `hello` within five seconds on two attempts in a
   row, or `connect-src` reports a violation, the page says "Live
   updates are off; refreshing every 3 seconds" and refetches `waiting`,
   the project lists and the open view every three seconds, applying by
   revision as before. It retries the socket on a reload only.
8. Send: `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}`, `op` a
   fresh UUID per attempt held until the reply; after a timeout the page
   reads `GET /api/v1/ops/{op}` and never resends blind (§4.5). Shown
   only when `device.scope` is `control`; a 403 `scope` hides it and
   re-reads `/device`. The 16 KiB cap is `info.limits.send_bytes`.
